# Voxelization via Rasterization


## Overview
Voxelization via Rasterization converts 3D geometric primitives (typically triangle meshes) into a discrete 3D voxel grid by leveraging the graphics pipeline's rasterization hardware [S1, unofficial]. It is distinguished from ray-marching or signed distance field (SDF) methods by its reliance on standard GPU rasterization primitives, though it may require specific techniques like conservative rasterization to avoid gaps [S1, unofficial].

## Shared principles
This family builds on the shared mechanism of converting scalar field data into geometric primitives submitted to the graphics pipeline [G]. See [Voxels rasterized as geometry](27-voxels-rasterized-as-geometry.md) for details on primitive generation, coordinate transformation, rasterization, and culling.

## Subtopics

### [3-axis rasterization voxelization](2480-3-axis-rasterization-voxelization.md)
This method converts 2D surface geometry into a 3D voxel grid by performing three separate rasterization passes along the axis-aligned directions (X, Y, and Z). It produces a **6-separating** voxelization, meaning the resulting voxel set is sparse enough to support 6-connected ray marching without penetrating the original surface. It is distinguished from 26-separating methods (which use full voxel cubes as intersection targets) by being significantly sparser, and from other 6-separating methods like Schwarz and Seidel [SS10] by being minimal, as it corresponds exactly to the "crosshairs" intersection target rather than a superset. See [3-axis rasterization voxelization](2480-3-axis-rasterization-voxelization.md).

### [Chunked UV Rasterization with Face ID Storage](2598-chunked-uv-rasterization-with-face-id-storage.md)
This method rasterizes a triangle mesh directly into a 2D UV texture space in memory-friendly chunks, storing the triangle (face) ID in the alpha channel of the resulting texture. This allows for per-texel face identification and subsequent interpolation of 3D vertex positions, effectively converting geometric mesh data into a volumetric representation without explicit ray marching or signed distance field computation. It differs from sibling methods like [3-axis rasterization](2480-3-axis-rasterization-voxelization.md) by processing faces in arbitrary batches rather than axis-aligned slices, and from [Triangle Projection Voxelization](5432-triangle-projection-voxelization.md) by explicitly managing VRAM constraints through chunked execution loops. See [Chunked UV Rasterization with Face ID Storage](2598-chunked-uv-rasterization-with-face-id-storage.md).

### [Triangle Projection Voxelization](5432-triangle-projection-voxelization.md)
Triangle Projection Voxelization renders input mesh triangles directly into a 3D voxel grid using a union-based accumulation strategy, where overlapping projections are resolved by retaining the maximum coverage or depth value. It differs from sibling methods like [3-axis rasterization voxelization](2480-3-axis-rasterization-voxelization.md) by treating the voxel grid as a volumetric render target rather than a set of discrete 2D slices, allowing for a single-pass (or few-pass) projection that inherently handles complex geometry intersections without explicit geometric clipping. See [Triangle Projection Voxelization](5432-triangle-projection-voxelization.md).

### [DX11.1 Forced Sample Count Optimization](8063-dx11-1-forced-sample-count-optimization.md)
This method leverages the DirectX 11.1 "Forced Sample Count" feature to perform Multi-Sample Anti-Aliasing (MSAA) rasterization without requiring a bound MSAA render target. It serves as a memory-efficient alternative to standard MSAA voxelization, which necessitates allocating an MSAA render target in video memory (vidmem). By decoupling the rasterization sample count from the render target format, it reduces vidmem overhead while providing coverage-based voxelization. See [DX11.1 Forced Sample Count Optimization](8063-dx11-1-forced-sample-count-optimization.md).

### Conservative Rasterization via Edge Expansion
- **Definition**: A technique to fix 'holes' introduced by switching projection directions in different primitives. Standard rasterization invokes the pixel shader only if a primitive covers the pixel center; this method expands primitive edges to ensure all pixels touched by the primitive are covered [S1, unofficial].
- **Step**: Expand primitive edges in the Geometry Shader to ensure all pixels touched by the primitive are covered by the rasterizer [S1, unofficial].
- **Pitfall**: Edge expansion causes extra pixels to be shaded (yellow pixels in Figure 9), particularly for thin triangles, leading to unnecessary pixel shader calls. These extra voxels must be culled later using voxel-primitive intersection tests [S1, unofficial].

### Hardware Conservative Rasterization
- **Definition**: Using hardware-supported conservative rasterization available on Maxwell base chipsets or higher via NVAPI. It avoids artifacts from manual edge expansion and eliminates the need for subsequent voxel-primitive intersection tests [S1, unofficial].
- **Parameter**: Hardware Requirement: Maxwell base chip set or higher [S1, unofficial].
- **Comparison**: Unlike manual edge expansion, hardware conservative rasterization does not produce extra shaded pixels, so voxel-primitive intersection tests are not needed [S1, unofficial].

## Background
The method originated from the need to efficiently voxelize triangle meshes for real-time global illumination and ray tracing on GPUs [G]. Early implementations relied on standard rasterization, which suffered from gaps ("holes") when primitives fell between pixel centers or when projection directions changed [S1, unofficial]. The introduction of conservative rasterization techniques, both manual (via geometry shader edge expansion) and hardware-supported (starting with NVIDIA's Maxwell architecture), provided robust solutions to these artifacts [S1, unofficial]. The technique is widely used in real-time rendering engines for voxel cone tracing, voxel-based lighting, and volumetric data visualization [G].
